reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the creator promotes crypto investment programs as a way to receive frequent, ongoing payouts, describing payments every few hours or minutes and saying that putting in more money yields more payouts. He urges viewers to get involved, set up accounts, and says he encourages buying a USI Tech package for upfront income; the risk disclaimer does not undo that direct solicitation. He also promotes referral-marketing help and commissions, but the central pitch is participation in the payout-generating crypto programs.

citations.quote: I'm literally getting paid out all day, every day.
my mining bot program and I don't really promote that because that's a high yield investment.
Get set up with your accounts, guys.
people want to make money off the referrals as well.
Put a lot of money in, you get paid out a lot.

opening.argument: The speaker explicitly distances himself from professional financial advice and tells viewers to limit exposure to what they can afford to lose: "I'm no guru, no financial advisor so I'm not telling you what to do" and "don't be willing to invest more than you are willing to lose." He also describes the mining-bot activity as a "high yield investment" that he does not want others entering. That framing is a personal-risk warning, not a representation that participation is guaranteed or suitable for everyone. The payout statements are presented as his own experience, while the express warning leaves the decision with the viewer.

citations.quote: I'm no guru, no financial advisor so I'm not telling you what to do
But don't be willing to invest more than you are willing to lose at the end of the day.
I don't really promote that because that's a high yield investment. I kind of put money in a while back and I just don't want anyone, you know, kind of going in that situation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account treats the payout language as if it were an unconditional promise, but the speaker expressly says he is not a financial adviser and warns against risking more than one can lose. Its quotation about setting up accounts also does not establish that viewers were promised a return; account creation and investment suitability are separate questions.

citations.quote: I'm no guru, no financial advisor so I'm not telling you what to do
don't be willing to invest more than you're willing to lose
Get set up with your accounts, guys.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A disclaimer does not neutralize the surrounding pitch. The speaker still says he is paid throughout the day, urges viewers to get involved, and encourages buying a package for income. Saying viewers should risk only what they can lose is compatible with promoting a risky scheme; it does not verify the programs or explain how the repeated payouts are funded.

citations.quote: I'm literally getting paid out all day, every day.
I still encourage you to buy a package so you can start generating some income upfront.

opening.argument: The content can be read as an operational explanation of how to use crypto-related marketing services, rather than a certification of investment safety. The speaker explains that funnels can perform selling and follow-up, describes directing people to training, and discusses switching currency from Coinbase to BTC or BitConnect. He presents TCP as useful because it helps users build programs and learn setup steps. That is instructional material about account and referral operations; the excerpts do not establish that he independently verified every external program or guaranteed a result.

you can direct them to a training system
show them how to set up their programs and how to actually purchase, switch currency over from Coinbase to BTC or to BITCONNECT
That's what I like about TCP

rebuttal.rebuttal: The recurring-payout excerpts show the speaker discussing his own crypto activity, but they do not eliminate the instructional subject matter. Explaining funnels, training systems, and currency conversion is materially different from certifying that an investment is safe or promising a particular outcome. The reference account also does not identify any false claim about the services being taught.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The instructional details are embedded in an appeal to join and fund crypto programs. The speaker says viewers should get involved, says funding is when "the magic begins," and encourages buying a package to generate income. A tutorial format does not change the fact that the lesson directs viewers toward payout-generating participation.

opening.argument: The identifiable services include marketing assistance, funnels, follow-up, and training for people seeking referrals. The speaker says he helps users set up funnels and directs people to training, which is consistent with ordinary promotional or business-support services. The supplied frames show the speaker talking from inside a car, not a displayed payment portal, credential collection, or transaction interface. The cited text also does not establish a guaranteed return, a required downline, or a specific compensation hierarchy. Referral commissions and service promotion alone do not prove that the promoted services are fraudulent.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The repeated-payout language is not merely ordinary service advertising: the speaker describes payments every three hours or every minute and links larger deposits to larger payouts. The absence of a payment screen in a sampled frame does not contradict spoken solicitation, and referral promotion is only one part of the presentation.

citations.quote: PowerMiner Pool pays me every three hours
miningBuy pays me every minute

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The record does show more than a neutral service: viewers are told to set up accounts, fund them, and buy packages for income. The fact that the sampled image lacks a payment interface does not address the spoken claims about frequent payouts or the invitation to participate. Ordinary referral assistance does not explain those investment-return claims.
